title: Human Physiology
lines: Human physiology is the largest biology topic in USAT-M. Questions ask where a process happens, which enzyme or hormone does a job, how blood flows through the heart, how the kidney makes urine, how nerve impulses travel, and how the body defends itself. Learn the tables; most questions are one-step recall.
## Digestion
| Region | Juice or enzyme | Action
| Mouth | salivary amylase | starch → maltose
| Stomach | HCl and pepsin (from pepsinogen) | HCl kills microbes and activates pepsin; proteins → polypeptides
| Duodenum | bile (from liver, stored in gall bladder) | emulsifies fat; has no enzyme
| Duodenum | pancreatic amylase, trypsin, lipase | starch → maltose; proteins → peptides; fats → fatty acids + glycerol
| Small intestine wall | maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases | disaccharides → monosaccharides; peptides → amino acids
- Absorption happens mainly in the ileum, through millions of villi. Sugars and amino acids enter the blood capillaries; fats enter the lacteals (lymph).
- The large intestine (colon) absorbs water and salts. Its bacteria make vitamin K.
- The liver makes bile, stores glycogen, turns excess amino acids into urea (deamination) and breaks down toxins.
- Gut hormones: gastrin (stomach) increases gastric juice; secretin and cholecystokinin (duodenum) stimulate the pancreas, and cholecystokinin also empties the gall bladder.
! Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase, not by HCl. Bile emulsifies fat but digests nothing.
## Blood and circulation

- Plasma (about 55 % of blood) carries dissolved food, CO₂, hormones and urea. Red cells carry O₂ on haemoglobin; mature red cells have no nucleus. White cells fight infection; platelets start clotting.
- ABO groups depend on antigens on red cells: group A has antigen A, B has B, AB has both, O has neither. O negative is the universal donor; AB positive is the universal recipient.

- The heart has four chambers. Deoxygenated blood: venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs. Oxygenated blood: pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → aorta → body. This is double circulation.
- The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood round the whole body.
- The beat starts in the sinoatrial (SA) node, the pacemaker in the right atrium. The impulse passes to the AV node, the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres.
- The first heart sound (lubb) is the closing of the AV valves; the second (dub) is the closing of the semilunar valves.

- Arteries have thick, elastic walls and carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Veins have thin walls and valves and carry blood back. Capillaries are one cell thick and exchange materials with tissues. Normal adult blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg.
> A person's heart beats 75 times a minute. How long is one cardiac cycle?
> 60 s ÷ 75 beats = 0.8 s per cycle.
> At this rate: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, complete diastole 0.4 s.
! The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. Arteries and veins are named by direction (away from or towards the heart), not by oxygen content.
## Breathing and gas exchange
- Air passes: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. C-shaped cartilage rings keep the trachea open.
- Gas exchange happens by diffusion across the thin, moist walls of millions of alveoli, which give a huge surface area.
- Inhaling: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs, chest volume rises, pressure falls and air rushes in. Quiet exhaling is mostly passive.
- About 97 % of O₂ travels as oxyhaemoglobin. Most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate ions in plasma. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than O₂, so it cuts O₂ transport.
- The breathing rate is controlled by the medulla, which responds mainly to the CO₂ level of the blood.
> Tidal volume is 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 3,000 mL and expiratory reserve volume 1,100 mL. Find the vital capacity.
> Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 500 + 3,000 + 1,100 = 4,600 mL.
> Residual volume is not included: it can never be breathed out.
## Excretion
- The kidneys remove urea, excess water and salts. Urea itself is made in the liver.

- The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney. Ultrafiltration happens from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule: water, glucose, salts and urea pass through, but blood cells and plasma proteins stay in the blood.
- Selective reabsorption: the proximal convoluted tubule takes back all the glucose and amino acids and most of the water and salts. The loop of Henle helps concentrate urine.

- Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released from the posterior pituitary, makes the collecting duct reabsorb more water, so less but more concentrated urine is made. Aldosterone increases Na⁺ reabsorption.
- Urine path: kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra.
> A patient's urine regularly contains glucose. What is the most likely reason?
> Normally all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
> In diabetes mellitus, blood glucose is so high that the filtered glucose exceeds what the tubule can reabsorb, so the extra appears in urine. Protein in urine instead points to damaged glomeruli.
## Nervous system and senses

- The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the nerves. A neuron has dendrites, a cell body and an axon, often covered by a myelin sheath that speeds conduction.
- At rest the inside of a neuron is about −70 mV. In an action potential, Na⁺ ions rush in (depolarisation), then K⁺ ions move out (repolarisation). The impulse is all-or-none.
- At a synapse a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine crosses the gap, so impulses travel in one direction only.
- Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle or gland).
| Brain part | Main job
| Cerebrum | thinking, memory, voluntary movement, senses
| Cerebellum | balance and coordination of movement
| Medulla oblongata | breathing, heart rate, blood pressure
| Hypothalamus | temperature, thirst, hunger; controls the pituitary

- Eye: in short sight (myopia) the image forms in front of the retina; it is corrected by a concave lens. In long sight (hypermetropia) the image forms behind the retina; a convex lens corrects it. Rods work in dim light; cones see colour.
## Endocrine system
| Gland | Hormone | Effect
| Pituitary (anterior) | growth hormone, TSH, FSH, LH | growth; controls other glands
| Pituitary (posterior) | ADH, oxytocin | water reabsorption; uterine contraction in childbirth
| Thyroid | thyroxine (contains iodine) | sets the metabolic rate
| Pancreas (islets of Langerhans) | insulin; glucagon | lowers blood glucose; raises it
| Adrenal medulla | adrenaline | fight or flight
| Testes | testosterone | male secondary sexual characters
| Ovaries | oestrogen, progesterone | female characters; maintain the uterus lining
The pituitary is called the master gland because it controls many other glands, but it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus. Lack of iodine causes goitre.
## Immunity
- Innate (non-specific) defences: skin, mucus, stomach acid, phagocytes and inflammation.

- Specific immunity uses lymphocytes. B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral immunity). T cells mature in the thymus; killer T cells destroy infected cells and helper T cells coordinate the response (cell-mediated immunity).
- Memory cells make the second response to the same antigen faster and stronger.

- Active immunity: the body makes its own antibodies after infection (natural) or vaccination (artificial). Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies from the mother through the placenta or milk (natural) or by injection (artificial). Passive immunity is quick but short-lived.
## Reproduction

- Male: sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, mature in the epididymis, and pass through the vas deferens and urethra. Seminal vesicles, the prostate and Cowper's glands add fluid.
- Female: an ovary releases an egg into the oviduct (Fallopian tube), where fertilisation happens. The embryo implants in the uterus.

- In a 28-day menstrual cycle, menstruation takes about days 1-5, FSH makes a follicle grow and secrete oestrogen, a surge of LH causes ovulation around day 14, and the corpus luteum then makes progesterone. If no pregnancy occurs, progesterone falls and menstruation starts again.
- Gametes are made by meiosis and carry 23 chromosomes; fertilisation restores 46.
! Many students write that the pituitary makes ADH. ADH is made in the hypothalamus and stored and released by the posterior pituitary; MCQs usually accept "posterior pituitary" as the source.
## Quick check
- Where does protein digestion begin? (stomach)
- Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle? (bicuspid or mitral)
- Which muscle flattens when you breathe in? (diaphragm)
- Where does ultrafiltration take place? (glomerulus into Bowman's capsule)
- Which ion rushes in during depolarisation? (Na⁺)
- Which hormone lowers blood glucose? (insulin)
- Antibodies from mother's milk give which immunity? (natural passive)
